title: Desert Island Psychiatry
subtitle: Lest we believe medicines are inessential.
body_html:
I recently wrote a book called Innessential Pharmacology (Amazon affiliate link). I suggest you buy it. It's good. It's also the number one book on Amazon in the depression and pharmacology categories, beating Michael Pollan’s “How to Change Your Mind.”

This is slightly hilarious to me. Also, based on the number two title, a lot of people need to prep for the pharmacy exam? I want to get into that game. If any of you Medical or Pharmacy students use my book to entertain yourself and you do better on an exam, please let me know.

That's like the gravy train for life. Given the sassy take on medications and the information about how to read science papers, my book might be helpful to those rotating as trainees through professional settings. For my general audience readers, rotations at a medical student are this kind of dreadful popularity contest. You're being graded by senior doctors based on your performance on the rotation, and some of them like to ask deeply embarrassing questions you're going to get wrong. We literally referred to this style of teaching as “PIMPing”—that's an acronym for “Put In My Place,” and like many things in medical training, it harkens back to an earlier era where being deeply shamed was understood as being what to expect. Except…that earlier Era is still the current Era for training in medicine.

We are moving on!

Carlene and I were talking. Yes, she is my wife. She wanted to make sure that I made the point that I don't think these medications are useless or that people should stop their medicines. To be clear, I don’t think this is the case. Many psychiatric medications are life-saving. Some of them have saved my life, personally. They are also fraught. So, she posed a question for me. “I'm gonna ask my readers as well.” If you had only five interventions, medicines, and procedures and had to practice Psychiatry on a desert island with no other resources, what would you want to have available and why?

Run into some issues of plausibility, of course. Do you get to have electricity on the desert island? Let's say yes. What about anesthesia? Well, that's gonna require separate drugs. You only get 5. I’m encouraging comments on this article to suggest your treatments and rationale. To get the conversation started, I’m going to start with this list of antipsychotics, which, to be clear, I’d want to have at least one of in my back pocket on a desert island.

Let the comments fly. If you were stuck somewhere and had to cover as much helping other people with as few treatments as possible, what would you pick, and why? I'm also asking this question to several colleagues, and it will become an article if you, dear readers, leave enough sassy comments. You're not limited to being a physician to answer these questions, as long as you have an opinion, and are willing to provide a rationale. I wrote a book about inessential medicines, but what are the essentials?
